I’m not really into competitive games, but Dota 2 is something else. All the heroes are cool, the game itself is excellent, and I genuinely have a great time playing positions 4 and 5. Mid is fun too, though. Man, my Skywrath Mage is something special.

One of the things I like most about Dota 2 is how much variety there is in the way you can play. The heroes feel distinct from one another, and even when two of them share some similarities, they can still offer completely different experiences. There are so many abilities, item combinations, and builds to experiment with that you can keep coming back to the same hero and still find new ways to play. Some heroes are flexible enough to fit into multiple positions, too, which makes things even more interesting. A hero's usual role doesn't necessarily have to be the only way to play them, and sometimes the fun comes from trying something that looks completely ridiculous on paper. I mean, come on, let me play Queen of Pain as a position 5. You can flame me all you want; I'm having fun.

The different builds are a big part of that appeal. You're not always locked into one specific way of playing a character, and adapting your items to the match can make a real difference. The facets also added another interesting layer to hero customization, giving you more reasons to experiment with different approaches. Whether they're still available in their original form or have changed over time, that kind of system is exactly what I enjoy about Dota 2: having more than one way to approach a hero instead of simply following the same build every game.

The hero leveling system is another nice touch. It's satisfying to level up your favorite characters, and the progression makes playing them feel even more rewarding. I especially like unlocking new chat wheel lines. There's something funny about having the perfect voice line ready for the right moment, whether you're celebrating a great play, teasing the enemy, or just being an absolute menace in chat. It's a small feature, but it gives you another reason to keep playing and makes your favorite heroes feel a little more personal.

The skins are great, and there's so much customization available for the heroes. Some combinations look fantastic, and putting together an appearance you really like is part of the fun in itself. And that Drow Ranger skin? Goodness gracious... As soon as I have some money to spare, I'm buying it. I might even buy two if I can. She looks so damn cool.

Of course, not everything about Dota 2 is great. The reporting system can be pretty frustrating, especially when it feels like people can spam reports against you and potentially get you penalized. Reports should be useful for dealing with genuinely disruptive behavior, not something players can abuse because they're angry about a match or don't like the way someone plays. There's a difference between deliberately ruining a game and picking an unconventional hero or trying an unusual build. If I'm playing Queen of Pain as a position 5, that might not be what you wanted to see in your match, but it doesn't automatically mean I'm trying to ruin it. Sometimes people just want to play differently, and the game gives them enough flexibility to make that interesting.

The matches themselves are another reason I enjoy the game. There are shorter modes for when you don't have much time to spare, but I think some of the best moments happen when a match goes on for a while. Games can become increasingly chaotic as both teams get stronger, and a match that seems decided can still turn around if someone makes a mistake or a team pulls off an incredible play. Those long games can be exhausting, of course, but there's something satisfying about a hard-fought match where every decision matters. Not every game needs to be a quick victory to be memorable.

There's a lot to learn, too. Between the heroes, abilities, items, matchups, positions, and all the different ways you can approach a game, there's always something new to figure out. Even after you've played for a while, you can still discover a build you hadn't considered or realize that a hero works better in a role you never expected. That depth is part of what makes Dota 2 so appealing to me. You don't necessarily need to be obsessed with competitive play to enjoy experimenting with the game and finding your own way to have fun.

Anyway, that's pretty much it. Dota 2 has its frustrating moments, and the community can certainly make things worse sometimes, but the sheer amount of variety, customization, and personality packed into the game makes it easy to understand why people keep coming back to it. I may not be the most competitive player around, but I know what I enjoy, and Dota 2 gives me plenty of reasons to keep playing.

When the game is playable, its actually not that bad and quite fun. However as as new dota player in the year 2026 there are several barriers holding you back from ever actually enjoying the game, and none of those barriers are related to the gameplay itself. The real fundamental problem’s I have with this game is the matchmaking and new player mode. 

I understand that having a new player on your team is frustrating, but I just don’t believe that them playing an ‘easier’ champion will at all fix the problem of them being new to the game. Just because someone is playing tidehunter instead of lycan in pos3, doesn’t mean they won’t still just be adjusting to the game. They still won’t understand pulling enemy melee minions to your ranged creep or what the enemy heros do, or about a thousand other macro/micro things to do with dota. I can understand that it may be easier to learn the game on an easier champ, but I think players should have the right to learn on whoever they want to learn on. I realize it’s easier just to hit R on tidehunter but if the player wants to play lycan I think they should be allowed to play lycan. What new player mode actually does is drive new players to not want to play the game since they can’t play the characters they want to play. 

Furthermore, the amount of bot lobbies I have encountered is just disgusting. What’s even worse, is when you get bots on your team but the enemy team gets not bots, leading to an unfair game state. Or when there are bots on each team and it comes to a challenge of which team can farm the bots better to get more gold. I don’t mean bots as a derogatory term by the way, truthfully they are bots created to sell accounts. I have got games before where they send out a message saying the game needs to go a certain length and to let them get some amount of kills for it to be counted so their accounts can be sold later on. 

It is very frustrating to attempt to play the game and you are just placed in bot lobby after bot lobby, this limbo where no matter how much you play you are eternally stuck not playing or really learning the game. Stomping bots is not how you learn the game, nor is it enjoyable in the slightest. I have never left a game or done anything to place myself into low prio q and my reputation score has only gone up since I started playing. However, I am still stuck in lobbies where I have bots on either my team the enemy team or both. In fact, with 99.3 hours played in a match, I am still receiving games where I am the only human in the lobby. 

In summary, I believe that when the game is playable, when there are no bots on your team or the enemy team, and you have a team willing to play their position the game is very enjoyable. However you really do have to suffer through at least 100 hours of just bot lobbies, which is disgusting, and also have to get through new player mode, which is just disheartening. I wish I could give a neutral review, since I still feel like despite having 162 hours in the game (this means 62 hours in queue, or 62 hours of uncounted games because yes sometimes bot lobbies aren't counted so you just waste time since leaving will put you in low prio q), just now is it becoming playable, which is unacceptable for how much this game is praised and put on a pedestal. I understand and get games taking a heavy commitment to get into, but I would rather get hard stomped by players better than me for 100 hours than just turn my brain off against bots.

Counter Strike 2...

I absolutely love this game; having played tons of fps games across many different platforms I can say that the Counter Strike franchise is my personal favorite for sure and it's not even close. Having only played CS2 myself I cannot speak for the other versions of the game (which from what I hear were better in some ways) but everything about the game CS:GO as a whole is perfect to me.

If you are looking to chill and have fun Counter Strike 2 has game modes and custom maps / lobbies that are well made and enjoyable - and also if you are looking to have a decent chance at losing your sanity and going absolutely ballistic you can also do it on CS2 as well with their more competitive game modes. Both the more casual and the more competitive game modes are tons of fun regardless of the capability they both have to make someone want to destroy their whole gaming setup! The sheer satisfaction of the game will keep you coming back for more time and time again.

The weapons and maps in this game are very well made and highly thoughtful; the maps actually make sense and have features or places on them that feel like they were actually designed to support pvp and the infinite combination of things that can happen. The same goes for the weapons, everything is pretty balanced and the meta feels more like a suggestion; people can do very well with just about any weapon and I've seen it time and time again, but still an AK or M4 is the top pick for most.

I would 100% recommend Counter Strike 2 to anyone who enjoys player vs player fps games, but I can say that the game is fairly difficult starting off. There's a lot of little things to learn and tips here and there that you'll end up getting along the way - so the start of the game will be a little painful until you get used to it. Once you get comfortable with the game it will stand out as one of the best if not the best competitive experiences you can have at the higher level of play. Nothing beats the feeling of a good match or a huge clutch or play and almost passing out due to your heart wanting to leave your body and your adrenaline soaring through the roof.

The Counter Strike atmosphere is amazing, the major events and tournaments are actually a blast to watch and the multiple pro scenes around the globe are interesting to follow and keep up with the players and teams. The weapon skin and case system are also nice to get into and actually have entire markets based around them. All in all once you dive in a little bit to the game and the stuff around it you start to enjoy the game a lot more and it will make you significantly better.

I love you Gabe Newell - Thank you for making this beautiful game and the CS:GO franchise.

This review is a little long, and it's not meant to be an analysis or critique of the game's gameplay or mechanics. This time, I want to share some memories I've made with Counter-Strike over the years. So, if you'd like to take a little trip down memory lane with me, then come along.

Some games are more than just a source of entertainment. Sometimes, they become tied to our memories, friendships, and even particular chapters of our lives. Counter-Strike is exactly one of those games for me.

My first encounter with the game goes back to my childhood, when I first visited a gaming café with my brother. Back then, my gaming world revolved around titles like Mortal Kombat, Tekken, Crash, and football games on the PlayStation 1 and 2, along with GTA: Vice City and San Andreas on PC. Among all those games, however, there was one that looked and played quite differently from the rest: a simple yet unique shooter that placed you on one of two opposing sides, Terrorists or Counter-Terrorists, with the objective of taking down the opposing team.
Years went by, and I eventually found my way back to those gaming cafés and that same game. This time, it was no longer just a new gaming experience. Counter-Strike gradually became part of my everyday teenage life. My friends, classmates, and I would make plans to meet up at the gaming café at a specific time, sometimes after school and sometimes after exams, just to play a few matches together. Those plans might have seemed simple and ordinary back then, but today, they've become some of the most unforgettable memories of that period of my life.
I had played so much by then that I had gradually become a pretty decent player. Being part of 5v5 matches and getting picked to form a team was nothing unusual anymore. I had practically become a regular choice whenever teams were being put together at the gaming café. Several years went by with Counter-Strike 1.6, years that became a significant part of my teenage memories.
Eventually, the day came when circumstances in life forced me to step away from the game. At the time, I might have thought it would only be temporary, but it turned into a much longer separation than I could have imagined.
Around 10 to 12 years have passed since those days. Now, I've found myself facing a new version of that same game. It has preserved its core identity and competitive spirit, but a lot has changed over the years. The graphics, maps, designs, items, and countless other details have all evolved with modern gaming standards. Counter-Strike is no longer just the simple game I remember from those days; it has grown into a massive and hugely popular franchise with a global following and major professional tournaments.

This year, I tried twice to get back into the game, even if only casually. But the truth is, I just couldn't find that same excitement I used to have. I don't know whether it's simply the passage of time and changing interests, or perhaps the magic of those days had less to do with the game itself and more to do with the people, circumstances, and atmosphere surrounding those experiences.
Maybe I can never relive those days again; the days when all it took was making plans with friends to play a few matches, and our biggest concern was simply having fun and competing against one another. Simple, carefree days, far removed from the complexities of life today.
Still, I want Counter-Strike to remain exactly as it lives in my memories. Not just as a game that has now received a newer version, but as a reminder of a time that will never come again. Maybe I'm no longer the player I used to be, but those memories are still with me.

Counter-Strike 2 – A Complete Disappointment

CS2 is honestly one of the biggest disappointments in the history of competitive gaming.

What happened to Counter-Strike? We went from having CS:GO, a game with personality, competitive integrity, and an incredible community, to this unfinished, frustrating mess called CS2.

Let's talk about the anti-cheat. VAC is an absolute joke. Cheaters are everywhere, blatant hackers can ruin entire matches, and legitimate players are left wasting their time. You can spend thousands of hours improving your aim, movement, and game sense, just to get destroyed by someone using cheats. The competitive experience is pathetic when you can't even trust the integrity of your matches.

Valve seems completely disconnected from its player base. We keep getting skins, cases, and cosmetic content, while one of the most important aspects of the game remains neglected: ACTUALLY STOPPING CHEATERS.

CS:GO had problems, but at least it felt like Counter-Strike. It had character, atmosphere, and an identity. CS2 feels like a soulless replacement that nobody asked to experience in this state. Source 2 was supposed to be an upgrade, but what did we really gain? Better graphics? For what, if the actual gameplay experience is constantly ruined?

The game that once represented competitive excellence now feels like an endless cycle of frustration:
- Useless anti-cheat against blatant cheaters.
- Unfair and frustrating matchmaking.
- A community losing patience.
- Updates that don't address the biggest problems.
- Valve prioritizing monetization while fundamental issues remain.

The most insulting part is that Counter-Strike has an enormous budget, a massive player base, and one of the most successful competitive gaming communities in history. Yet players still have to beg for basic competitive integrity.

CS2 isn't the evolution of CS:GO. It feels like a downgrade wearing a new coat of paint.

I don't care about another case, another skin collection, or another meaningless cosmetic update. FIX THE ANTI-CHEAT. FIX THE GAME.

Counter-Strike used to be a legend. Now it's a frustrating reminder of what happens when developers take their loyal community for granted.

The core idea is simple that you place two linked portals and use them to get through puzzles. But the game keeps adding new tools at a steady pace such as light bridges, tractor beams and paint like gels that make you bounce or speed along. Just as you’ve mastered one mechanic, it gives you a new one to combine with the rest. The puzzles are clever without being unfair and the moment a solution clicks makes you feel smart rather than just lucky.

The writing is the other big reason I love it. The characters are funnier and sharper than ever. The character voiced by J.K. Simmons steals every scene he’s in. The game is funny and it still manages to tell a surprisingly strong story with enjoyable twists and a fantastic ending.

The co-op campaign deserves its own praise. You have to plan, communicate and sometimes troll each other. It’s a solid and enjoyable co-op experience and feels like a whole second game.

The presentation holds up well too. The environments are full of detail, the soundtrack reacts to what you’re doing and the game runs well on almost any machine. Add years of community made levels and there’s a huge amount to enjoy.

Portal 2 is smart, funny and endlessly inventive. If you’ve never played it, it’s an easy recommendation.

Two Legendary Games That Never Get Old — GIVE US LEFT 4 DEAD 3!

As a longtime, die-hard *Left 4 Dead* fan, I can honestly say that Left 4 Dead 1 and 2 are two of the greatest zombie games ever made. Even after all these years, I still come back to them, and somehow, they never get old.

There is just something special about these games that modern zombie shooters still struggle to capture. The frantic gameplay, the teamwork, the panic when a horde comes rushing toward you, and that one friend who ALWAYS manages to get everyone killed. 😂

Every campaign can turn into a completely different experience. One minute, your team is cruising along like a well-oiled machine, and the next, a Tank shows up, a Smoker drags someone away, a Hunter pounces on your buddy, and the entire plan falls apart in seconds. Those unpredictable moments are what make these games so damn memorable.

The Modding Community Keeps These Games Alive

One of my favorite things about Left 4 Dead 1 and 2 is the modding community. The amount of creativity players have brought to these games is incredible. Custom campaigns, weapons, character models, sound effects, visual changes, and all kinds of ridiculous modifications give you endless ways to change up the experience.

Even after years of playing, there's always something new to try. The community has helped keep these games alive long after their original releases, and that's a testament to how fantastic the foundation is.

And then there's Crowd Control, which takes the chaos to a whole new level!

I absolutely love using Crowd Control to let my Steam chat spawn zombies into my game. Instead of simply watching me play, viewers can actively make my life miserable by unleashing more undead when I least expect it. 😂

Trying to survive a campaign while your own viewers are plotting your demise is an absolute blast. You think you've got everything under control, then chat decides it's time to ruin your day. It creates hilarious, unpredictable moments and makes streaming these games even more entertaining.

Honestly, this kind of community interaction is one of the reasons I keep coming back. The game is already chaotic enough on its own, but letting viewers influence the action makes every run feel like a new adventure.

So… Where the Hell Is Left 4 Dead 3?

This is my biggest wish: I desperately want a proper Left 4 Dead 3.

Imagine a modern sequel with updated graphics, improved animations, more detailed environments, new special infected, fresh campaigns, and all the intense cooperative gameplay that made the originals legendary.

Give us new survivors to get attached to, new locations to explore, new ways to get absolutely destroyed by the infected, and a campaign experience that captures the atmosphere and tension of the original games.

And please, keep the modding support! Let the community continue creating custom content and give us tools to make the game our own. Imagine what modders could accomplish with a modern Left 4 Dead game.

If Valve isn't going to make a third game, then at the very least, give us proper remakes of the originals. Keep the classic campaigns, preserve the gameplay that made them special, and bring them into the modern era with updated visuals, improved performance, and better tools for the community.

I don't want the soul of these games changed. I want the same incredible experience, just brought up to modern standards.

Final Verdict: Absolute Classics

Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2 are timeless zombie-shooter classics. The gameplay is addictive, the replayability is incredible, the modding community is amazing, and the ability to create complete chaos with Crowd Control makes them even better.

These games prove that you don't need a massive open world, an endless progression system, or a complicated live-service model to create something people will love for years. Sometimes, all you need is a group of survivors, a few guns, a horde of zombies, and a Tank waiting around the next corner.

Recommended without hesitation.

Thousands of hours? Maybe not quite. Countless memories? Absolutely. And I'm still here, shooting zombies and letting my chat make my life miserable.

Valve, please… GIVE US LEFT 4 DEAD 3! And if that's too much to ask, at least give these legendary games the remakes they deserve.
